title: Cls Wallet
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Question ID: 14724_cls_wallet

During a crowded Christian law-student fellowship worship night in a law-school auditorium, Daniel saw a wallet fall out of Lydia’s purse. Daniel picked up the wallet and found that it contained $100 in cash. Thinking that he could use the money and seeing no one watching, Daniel put the wallet in the pocket of his coat. Just then, Lydia approached Daniel and asked whether he had seen a missing wallet. Daniel said no and went home with the wallet.

Of what crime, if any, is Daniel guilty?
call: Of what crime, if any, is Daniel guilty?
rightExplanation:
C is correct. Daniel took and carried away Lydia’s wallet after seeing it fall from her purse, knowing it belonged to someone nearby and intending to keep it. Gold Key: A finder commits larceny when, at the time he takes found property, he knows or has a practical way to identify the owner and intends to keep it. The lie after Lydia asks for the wallet confirms the original keep-it intent; it does not create false pretenses because Lydia never transferred title to Daniel.

Silver Key: In a theft-label answer set, do not ask which label sounds most criminal. Ask how Daniel got the property: no entrustment, no title transfer, direct taking of another’s property.

c3.label: CUT
c3.text: No purely grammatical cut exists because the choices are bare crime labels.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text: The answer array is a theft-label identity set: embezzlement vs false pretenses vs larceny vs no crime.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: Use the Gold Key. The stem shows no entrustment, no title transfer, and an owner-identifiable taking with intent to keep. Residual answer: C. Larceny.

studentScript: Wallet fell from Lydia. Daniel saw it, took it, planned to keep it, lied, and left. No entrustment means not embezzlement. No title transfer means not false pretenses. Not no crime because the owner was identifiable and he intended to keep it. Larceny.

A.signal: The stem says Daniel found the wallet after it fell; Lydia never handed it to him to hold.
A.lawyer: Embezzlement requires property entrusted to the defendant or lawful possession later fraudulently converted.

B.signal: Daniel's lie came after he already had the wallet; Lydia did not transfer ownership because of the lie.
B.lawyer: False pretenses requires obtaining title through misrepresentation.

C.signal: The stem gives taking, property of another, owner nearby, and intent to keep.
C.lawyer: Common-law larceny is the trespassory taking and carrying away of another's personal property with intent to permanently deprive.

D.signal: The stem does not show innocent finding; it shows owner-identifiable property plus concealment and lie.
D.lawyer: Under the tested rule, this is larceny; the finder’s later denial confirms the intent to deprive.

goldKeys.statement: For theft labels, ask how the defendant got the property: trespassory taking = larceny; entrusted possession later converted = embezzlement; title obtained by lie = false pretenses.
goldKeys.trigger: Answer choices are bare theft labels and the stem shows a found item, later lie, or transfer path.
goldKeys.unlocks: larceny vs embezzlement vs false pretenses vs no-crime trap
goldKeys.authority: Lawyer-confirmation only: common-law larceny definitions; embezzlement entrusted-property distinction; false-pretenses title-transfer distinction.

silverKeys.statement: When choices are bare theft labels, map the stem’s transfer path before ranking the labels.
silverKeys.trigger: Choices are Embezzlement / False pretenses / Larceny / No crime.

remediation.title: Theft labels: possession path first
remediation.studentMove: Ask how the defendant got the property before choosing a label.
remediation.tinyRule: Found/taken + intent to keep points to larceny; entrusted points to embezzlement; title-by-lie points to false pretenses.
remediation.trap: Picking the label that sounds most familiar instead of matching the transfer path.
